title: Tenant can make the platform sign another tenant's business-asset key
description: The kiosk branding server action forwards the caller's object to updateBranding without narrowing it, and brandingSchema accepts logo_key and kiosk video_key as free-form strings. updateBranding stores them and the public kiosk config signs them with the service role in the shared business-assets bucket, so a member of tenant A can persist tenant B's object key and then receive a working signed URL for it.
claimed_root_cause: Storage keys are accepted from client input and signed without checking that the key belongs to the caller's business prefix.

trace.description: Server action receives a caller-supplied object typed with welcome/colour/kiosk fields; TypeScript types are erased at runtime.
Everything except reset_pages is spread into payload, so an extra logo_key or kiosk.video_key supplied by the caller survives.
payload is parsed with brandingSchema, which allows logo_key and kiosk video_key but performs no ownership check.
The merged branding, including the foreign key, is written to business_settings.branding.
getPublicConfig signs logo_key and video keys with the service role in the business-assets bucket and returns the URLs to an unauthenticated caller.

evidence.description: logo_key is a plain optional string with a 300-character cap; no prefix or business check.
kiosk video_key has the same free-form shape.
logoSignedUrl signs whatever key it is given via loadSignedUrl(BRAND_ASSETS_BUCKET, key).
signedUrls batches keys into signedUrlMap for the shared business-assets bucket without any prefix filter.
The signed logo URL is part of the unauthenticated public kiosk config, so an object key can be learned from any booth page.

blockers: No local Supabase project or object store is available in this environment, so the signed fetch of a foreign key could not be executed and observed.
Whether the deployed bucket policy narrows signed reads by prefix is a storage configuration fact that source cannot establish.

validation_plan.local: With a local Supabase stack and two dummy businesses, create business A and business B, upload a logo for B, read B's public config to obtain its logo_key, then call saveBrandingKioskAction as a member of A with logo_key set to B's key and fetch A's public config. A working signed URL for B's object confirms the cross-tenant read.
validation_plan.deployment: Ask the storage owner whether the business-assets bucket or its R2 equivalent restricts signed URL issuance to a business prefix; if it does not, the signed URL returned for a foreign key is the confirmation.

title: Device report could store script in device_status
description: A device token holder posts camera and printer diagnostics that are merged into photoboxes.device_status and shown in the owner dashboard, which raised the question of stored script execution.
claimed_root_cause: A device can write arbitrary JSON into a field the owner dashboard renders.

trace.description: Public route accepts a device report payload.
Camera and printer sub-objects are merged into device_status.

evidence.description: camera is a strict object with resolution (40 chars), width (integer) and error (200 chars); printer is limited to confirmed, last_test_at, mode enum and device_name (60 chars).
The report schema has no free-form record field, so no arbitrary keys or markup-bearing structures can be stored.

reason: The payload shape is fixed and length-bounded, and the dashboard renders these values through React text nodes, so no script context is reachable. This is a refuted candidate, not a hardening note.

title: Device can act on a checkout belonging to another booth
description: createPayment, applyVoucherToCheckout and abortSession load the checkout or session by business only and do not compare checkout.photobox_id with the authenticated device's photobox.
claimed_root_cause: Missing per-booth binding lets a device act on a sibling booth's checkout.

trace.description: Checkout is loaded with the device's businessId only.
The query filters by id and business_id but not by photobox_id.

evidence.description: Session finalize and abort do compare session.photobox_id with the device, so the sensitive media path is bound; the checkout-only paths move no data across principals.
The device must still belong to the same business, and both booths are owned by the same tenant, so no tenant boundary is crossed.

reason: The affected resources belong to the same business and the same principal, and money still flows to that business's own credential. This is intra-tenant state confusion, not a boundary violation; it is recorded as a hardening note instead of a finding.

title: Voucher usage_limit is enforced at checkout creation, not at settlement
description: validateVoucherForCheckout rejects a voucher only when voucher_usages already contains usage_limit rows. Those rows are written during settlement, so several open checkouts that all reference the same voucher can each be paid and each insert a usage row, exceeding the owner's configured limit.
claimed_root_cause: The settlement path inserts voucher_usages without re-checking vouchers.usage_limit, so the limit only counts already-settled redemptions at the moment a checkout is created.

trace.description: Voucher eligibility is validated once, while the checkout is created and still unpaid.
The limit is compared against a count of voucher_usages rows; rows do not exist yet for any open checkout.
After payment is confirmed, settlement is delegated to the settle_paid_payment_atomically database function.
The function inserts a voucher_usages row whenever the payment carries a voucher_id, with no usage_limit read or check.

evidence.description: usage_limit is enforced only inside create_voucher_payment_atomically, the zero-amount voucher path, which locks the voucher row and counts usages.
vouchers.usage_limit is a plain nullable integer with no database-level enforcement.
expireStaleCheckoutsForPhotobox keeps one open checkout per booth, so the number of simultaneous redemptions scales with the number of booths in the business.

blockers: No local Postgres/Supabase instance is available, so two concurrent settlements against one voucher could not be executed to observe the second insert.
Whether a deployment trigger or policy outside db/schema.sql enforces the limit is a database configuration fact not visible in the repository.

validation_plan.local: On a local Supabase stack, seed one voucher with usage_limit = 1 and two booths. Create one checkout with the voucher on each booth, pay both through the cash or gateway path, then count voucher_usages for that voucher; two rows confirm the bypass.
validation_plan.deployment: Ask the database owner to run select count(*) from voucher_usages where voucher_id = '<id>' for a voucher whose usage_limit is 1 and that was offered on multiple booths during one campaign.

title: Rate-limit key trusts a client-settable forwarding header
description: getClientIp returns cf-connecting-ip before any proxy-verified header. The shipped nginx configuration sets X-Real-IP and X-Forwarded-For but neither sets nor strips cf-connecting-ip, so on that deployment a caller can rotate the header per request and never share a rate-limit bucket.
claimed_root_cause: A header that the requester can supply is treated as a trusted client identity for every per-IP rate limit.

trace.description: cf-connecting-ip is returned first, before x-real-ip and x-forwarded-for.
The login IP limit is keyed on that value.
Activation-code attempts are limited only per that IP value.
The derived value becomes the Redis or in-memory counter key, so a new value means a fresh bucket.

evidence.description: nginx sets X-Real-IP from $remote_addr but does not touch cf-connecting-ip.
X-Forwarded-For is appended to, so the client-supplied cf-connecting-ip still passes through.
x-real-ip and x-forwarded-for are only consulted when cf-connecting-ip is absent, so the proxy-set headers never override a supplied one.

blockers: Whether a CDN in front of the origin overwrites cf-connecting-ip is a deployment fact that source cannot establish.
No HTTP edge is running in this environment, so header handling by the actual proxy chain could not be observed.

validation_plan.local: Run the app behind the shipped nginx config on loopback and send 50 login or activation requests with a different cf-connecting-ip each time; absence of a 429 while the same requests with a fixed header are limited confirms the bypass.
validation_plan.deployment: Ask the operator whether requests reach the origin through Cloudflare (which overwrites the header) or directly; if directly, capture one request at the origin and check that cf-connecting-ip equals the value the client sent.
